video_title: The Market Is Mispricing The Inevitable | Peter Tchir
gist: Peter Tchir, head of macro strategy at Academy Securities, argues large asset managers still refuse to believe deglobalization and 'production for security' (his ProSec trade) are permanent, and are mispricing it as a post-midterms fad. His actionable book: long high-grade corporate credit (LQD) over long treasuries (zero interest in TLT), long the 2-year via TUA, overweight processing/refining, nuclear, energy, Canada, Europe, Poland and Central/South America, and heavily underweight semis/AI where cheap Chinese compute threatens the earnings assumption underpinning US index valuations.

themes.theme: Warsh Fed and the inflation-data regime change

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh's Fed data task force is the most consequential Fed initiative in years because he will keep the same reaction function but feed it broader, more real-time data than official BLS/CPI/PCE series.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir, head of macro strategy, Academy Securities
insights.so_what: If the Fed's inputs change rather than its rules, positioning built around printed CPI/PCE prints will misread Fed reaction; watch for official Fed commentary discrediting OER and lagged shelter data.
insights.quote: I think Wars' reaction function is not going to be that different than prior Feds. He's just going to look at different data to get that reaction function.

insights.claim: Official inflation measures are structurally biased by owner's equivalent rent — an estimate of what a single-family home would rent for, sampled at only about one-tenth of homes per period — making shelter inflation a lagging fiction.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Alternative real-time series (Truflation, Zillow rents) are what corporations and hedge funds actually trade off; expect official inflation to converge downward toward them.

insights.claim: The Fed made a symmetric error: too easy in 2020-2021 when official CPI understated real-time inflation, and now too tight because the same flawed metrics overstate it.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Frames the current setup as a policy-error-in-reverse trade: front-end rates too high relative to true inflation.
insights.quote: now I think we're making the mistake in the opposite direction

insights.claim: Bernanke's promotion of PCE as the preferred gauge was convenient because PCE stayed below 2% for decades, enabling easy money; now that PCE sits above 2% the metric's usefulness is being questioned from the other side.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Suggests the target metric itself may be revisited under Warsh — a regime shift markets are not pricing.
insights.quote: I think why he liked PCE was PCE never goes above 2%.

insights.claim: Rate hikes cannot fix today's two inflation sources — the Iran war's effect on oil and the AI/data-center buildout — because AI capex expecting 20-30x returns is insensitive to 25-50bp of policy rate.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Base case of no hike; fade market pricing of tightening and own the front end.
insights.quote: these companies trying to build out the AI, they think they're going to make 20x, 30x, 25 bips or 50 bips on rates is not going to slow that down

insights.claim: A Warsh-era balance sheet policy will likely become adaptive rather than prescriptive — the Fed could stop mechanically buying $25bn/month of treasuries and even sell treasuries if prices get too high.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Two-way balance sheet policy caps duration rallies and adds a new source of long-end volatility.

themes.theme: Curve, treasury demand erosion and the corporate-over-sovereign trade

insights.claim: The 10-year treasury is range-bound at roughly 4.5% to 5% with a persistently steeper curve, so the money is in the two-year rather than the long end.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Steepeners and front-end duration over long duration; a break below 4.5% requires an economic shock, not a Fed pivot.
insights.quote: I think it's going to be difficult to get 10 years below four and a half%. I don't think they go crazy above 5%.

insights.claim: Tchir is long and will add to TUA, a leveraged-duration two-year treasury ETF that uses futures to amplify two-year exposure, as the cleanest expression of a no-hike front-end view.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A named, specific vehicle for the front-end trade — note he flags it as aggressive.
insights.quote: So, if you're aggressive on this, like own some Tua and I will probably add to it.

insights.claim: Treasuries have lost gold-standard status and become 'generic' because Middle East petro-buyers have flipped from large net buyers to smaller buyers and even issuers, global sovereigns are issuing more defense debt, and foreign investors are politically annoyed at Trump.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Structural demand erosion argues for a permanent term-premium floor at the long end regardless of Fed policy.
insights.quote: they just aren't the gold standard they once were

insights.claim: High-grade AI-hyperscaler corporate debt should be owned overweight versus sovereign debt because the excess spread is unwarranted given their cash generation and superior corporate governance relative to a US government that periodically threatens default at the debt ceiling.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Own LQD, not TLT; the crowding-out fear that widened hyperscaler spreads is the entry point, not the risk.
insights.quote: I think you're being overcompensated for the risk.

insights.claim: Tchir has zero interest in owning TLT (20-30 year treasuries) and prefers LQD long-dated corporate credit yielding close to or above 6%, explicitly accepting the growing hyperscaler concentration inside that index.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A concrete relative-value pair trade: long LQD / avoid TLT, with the yield pickup as carry.
insights.quote: I have zero interest right now in being long TLT.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler equity is the vulnerable leg of the AI trade while hyperscaler debt is protected — if the data-center story slows, valuations compress but cash flow and asset-sale capacity still cover the bonds.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Capital-structure arbitrage: express AI skepticism by rotating from mega-cap equity into mega-cap credit rather than shorting.
insights.quote: if anything slows down in the data center AI story, their equities could face pressure because they will have a valuation issue

insights.claim: Alternative asset managers are a recovery play because stabilizing credit conditions turn the private-credit narrative from a fear story back into an attractive carry story; Tchir cites an ETF he calls GPZ that holds the alt managers.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A contrarian long on the most-shorted corner of financials if the private-credit scare fades; verify the exact ticker before acting.

themes.theme: Iran war endgame, oil and depleted strategic reserves

insights.claim: Academy Securities' network of roughly 30 retired generals, admirals and CIA officers believes the military has told the president that further strikes on Iran cannot produce regime change, so major escalation is off the table and the campaign will quietly fade into a declared win by September.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Argues for fading the war-risk premium in oil and rates into late Q3 rather than chasing escalation headlines.
insights.quote: my base case is that somehow we slowly stop talking about this

insights.claim: Gulf states are privately telling Washington to back off because US air defense stops only 90-95% of incoming fire, leaving 5-10% to hit their infrastructure, and they fear Iran will target Gulf energy assets in retaliation.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Gulf capitulation caps US escalation and means Iranian deterrence via missiles persists — a permanent risk premium on Gulf energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Global strategic petroleum reserves, not spare production, absorbed the first three months of the Iran war and are now largely exhausted — the US SPR is under 300 million barrels near what experts consider the limit, Europe has drained much of its stock, and China has returned to buying oil in the open market.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: The shock absorber that suppressed crude is gone; the next supply disruption transmits straight into price, and distillates/chemicals are the tightest link.
insights.quote: the US is now down to under 300 million barrels I believe in our strategic petroleum reserve

insights.claim: The pivot to unprecedented economic sanctions on Iran will fail because sanctions only bite if the US is willing to punish China for trading with Iran — and doing so would be far worse for the global economy than the war itself.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Sanctions headlines are noise unless secondary sanctions on China appear — that specific escalation is the real tail risk to price.
insights.quote: how do you stop Iran economically if you're not going to stop Iran trading with China? And that is a huge step.

insights.claim: The negotiated MOU with Iran was so weak that an Academy intelligence officer was nearly in tears reading it, and sending Witkoff and Kushner rather than nuclear PhDs and engineers cost the US the technical leverage it had won militarily.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Diplomatic failure means the Iran overhang recurs rather than resolves — treat any 'deal' rally in risk assets as temporary.
insights.quote: Iran has never won a war but they've never lost a negotiation and they seem to be right back at that

insights.claim: Gulf states collectively own more F-35s than Israel does yet are not flying them or using their weapons against Iran, revealing capitulation rather than any appetite for a regional coalition to box Iran in.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Hardware inventories overstate regional deterrence; do not model a Gulf-led containment of Iran.
insights.quote: Combined there are probably more F-35s I think in the region owned by the Gulf States than there are by Israel. And yet they're not flying them.

insights.claim: Regime change in Iran through popular uprising is far harder than historical analogies suggest because the modern security apparatus holds weapons effectively of mass destruction while civilians do not — the same logic that makes a Putin or North Korean overthrow implausible.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Kills the 'regime change unlocks Iranian barrels' bull case for oil supply; the IRGC has every incentive to prolong the conflict.
insights.quote: the IRGC is really still in power the IRGC has every incentive to keep this going so I I I think it's going to fail

insights.claim: The US is six months to a year away from fielding true asymmetric drone warfare capability, and is currently burning exquisite expensive missile systems to shoot down cheap drones.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A multi-quarter, government-funded procurement runway for domestic drone and counter-drone manufacturers; cost-exchange-ratio failure is the forcing function.
insights.quote: we're not yet flooding the zone with our own drones and and that's kind of shocking

insights.claim: North Korea's unusual silence is itself the warning signal, and its role rearming Iran plus its nuclear stockpile makes a North Korean nuke reaching Iran the worst-case scenario nobody is pricing.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: An unpriced geopolitical tail; quiet from Pyongyang should raise rather than lower risk budgets.
insights.quote: it's like when your kids are in the other room and you don't hear them, you should be more concerned than otherwise

themes.theme: Choke points, tail risk and supply-chain re-rating

insights.claim: Academy Securities maps 13 global maritime choke points and the map is drawing unusual client attention because drone technology has made blocking a trade zone cheap and easy — offense now decisively beats defense.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Shipping insurance, freight rates and inventory buffers are structurally repriced higher; the Hormuz toll model is replicable elsewhere.
insights.quote: It's much easier to destroy things right now than it is to defend.

insights.claim: China can throttle the Strait of Malacca with grey-zone tactics alone — tens of thousands of maritime militia fishing boats throwing logs and nets to foul propellers, as already practiced against the Philippines — without ever firing a shot.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Corporate supply-chain war-gaming that was laughed at two years ago is now standard, which itself drives the reshoring capex cycle.

insights.claim: The decisive change is behavioral: corporations now assign non-zero probability to tail scenarios like a Chinese blockade of Malacca, so lowest cost is no longer the sole sourcing determinant and risk weighting is being added to procurement.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: This is the mechanism that makes reshoring capex durable rather than a policy fad — margin compression for importers, revenue for domestic producers.
insights.quote: I think the cheapest cost is no longer going to be the sole determinant

insights.claim: 'Tyranny of distance' from the new national security strategy — a 32-page, double-spaced document — implies the US will concentrate supply chains in Central and South America where it has control and China has less influence.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A Monroe-Doctrine-2.0 nearshoring bid for Latin American infrastructure, logistics and resource assets.

insights.claim: Building pipelines around the Strait of Hormuz is naive because Iran retains missile and drone capacity, so any usable Saudi bypass pipeline must be hardened or underground — permanently raising the cost of doing business in the region.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Discount the bypass-pipeline fix that bulls cite; Gulf energy carries a structurally higher cost of capital.

themes.theme: ProSec: government wallet as industrial policy

insights.claim: Large asset managers still refuse to believe globalization is over — many senior allocators rose to their positions by embracing globalization and assume production-for-security fades after the midterms — which is precisely the mispricing.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: The core edge of the episode: institutional capital is under-allocated to reshoring beneficiaries because of career-formed priors, not analysis.
insights.quote: there's still a reluctance almost to believe that the end of global trade um and globalization is over

insights.claim: Washington is shifting from subsidies to direct procurement leverage — 100% tariffs on drones announced Friday, DoD data centers on federal land barred from using Chinese components, and seven-year contracts to defense manufacturers so they will build new factories.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Multi-year contract visibility converts defense/drone capex from cyclical to contracted revenue — a re-rating catalyst for domestic primes and suppliers.

insights.claim: Federal land is the unlock for data centers and small nuclear because the government can bypass not-in-my-backyard opposition, and the DoD is both building its own data centers and doing joint ventures on its property.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: States with large federal/military land holdings capture disproportionate AI-infrastructure and nuclear buildout.

insights.claim: The next phase of industrial policy is conditional spending and equity stakes: after price floors like the MP Materials magnet deal, expect requirements such as 80% American components or 50% US steel attached to federal contracts, plus more direct US government ownership in companies.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Domestic content thresholds create winner-take-most dynamics for compliant suppliers and strand importers; watch for the framework governing state ownership.
insights.quote: I think we're going to see more direct investment from the US government into companies

insights.claim: Today's industrial policy is a reversion to Cold War norm rather than an aberration — the US ran 36 open arsenals during the Soviet standoff and dismantled that capacity as a peace dividend, leaving it exposed.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Historical framing that argues the reshoring regime persists across administrations, not just this term.
insights.quote: I think it's a reversion almost to the norm

insights.claim: Government incentive-prize structures work: SpaceX became a multi-trillion-dollar company on the back of NASA-alternative monetization programs, and four companies just hit a federal challenge to take new nuclear reactor designs critical by July 4, 2026.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir and Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Prize-linked federal programs are a repeatable screen for identifying the next subsidized winner in energy and defense tech.

themes.theme: Processing, refining and the physical bottleneck trade

insights.claim: The bottleneck in critical minerals is not extraction but processing — China controls about 60% of extraction of rare earths and critical minerals but roughly 90% of processing and refining.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Position in processors, refiners and smelters rather than pure miners; that is where the scarcity rent accrues first.
insights.quote: China only controls about 60% of the extraction of those. They control 90% of the processing refining.

insights.claim: Tchir prefers processing and refining companies over the commodities themselves in his own portfolio, calling that the big shortcoming of the Western supply chain.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A specific allocation instruction: midstream/processing equity over spot commodity exposure.
insights.quote: I want to have a higher uh potential really around the companies that are going to process and refine this because that's really the big shortcoming

insights.claim: Australia announcing its first new refinery in 60 years is a bigger signal than it appears, because the US has not built a brand new refinery in 40 years — only rebuilt on existing footprints.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: First-mover refinery capacity in allied countries is the leading indicator that the reshoring capex cycle is real; watch for a US follow-on announcement.
insights.quote: I don't think the US has actually built a brand new refinery in 40 years

insights.claim: Every country is concluding it cannot rely on China, the Middle East, or even the US, and will move toward vertically integrated nationhood with domestic capacity in electricity, energy and chips.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Global, not just US, capex on power and chips — the addressable market for reshoring suppliers is multi-country.
insights.quote: Every country is kind of coming to this eye openening conclusion that you certainly cannot rely on China for everything

themes.theme: Nuclear, power and the reshaping of US real estate

insights.claim: Small and micro nuclear reactors are the highest-conviction long-duration holding Tchir wants to buy and forget for two to three years, and he owns both SMR names and uranium despite poor recent performance.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: An explicitly patient position sized for a multi-year federal-land deployment cycle, not a momentum trade.
insights.quote: that's a part that I just want to close my eyes and look at again in two or three years

insights.claim: Nuclear's obstacle is marketing and community outreach, not technology or safety — the US Navy has operated roughly 50-odd nuclear-powered ships and submarines for decades, a precedent the industry has failed to leverage.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Sentiment, not physics, is the gating factor — a narrative shift is the catalyst that re-rates the sector.
insights.quote: if only the nuclear energy could have hired the Bitcoin marketing team, we'd have nuclear energy everywhere instead of Bitcoin

insights.claim: The Great Lakes and Midwest are the emerging winners in US real estate over California, New York and Florida because they have electricity, fresh water, underused interstates built for old production towns, and extreme affordability.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A concrete regional CRE and industrial-property rotation driven by power and water access rather than migration trends.
insights.quote: I'm more and more comfortable in the Great Lakes and the Midwest than I am necessarily California, New York, Florida

insights.claim: State-level political willingness is becoming the swing variable for the AI buildout — one report Tchir cites argues the data-center AI trade comes down to the Texas governor election, and Wisconsin is already seeing pushback on some data center projects.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: State elections and permitting fights are an underfollowed catalyst calendar for data-center and power names.
insights.quote: They think the data center AI trade comes down to the um Texas governor election.

insights.claim: Framing the China economic competition as a national mission is generating genuine worker buy-in — Arizona power company employees told Academy they were proud to feel part of something bigger than supplying electricity to TSMC.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Soft evidence that the reshoring narrative has political durability beyond one administration — supports the 'this is not a midterms fad' thesis.

themes.theme: China AI catch-up and underweighting semis

insights.claim: Cheap Chinese compute is arriving faster than expected and Deep Seek was not a one-off — average-quality AI is catching up while China distills its models on Western IP, eroding the US lead Tchir thought was larger.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: The most direct threat to US AI pricing power and therefore to the index-level earnings assumption; a genuine change of mind from a macro strategist.
insights.quote: I've been a little bit caught by surprise um how quickly cheap Chinese compute is coming on the market

insights.claim: LLMs may converge to roughly the same capability level, in which case China wins on cost because it has multiples more electricity generation, cheaper chips at scale, no not-in-my-backyard constraints, and more engineers.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: If model quality commoditizes, the moat shifts to energy cost — bearish AI-model margins, bullish power.
insights.quote: there is some potential that LLMs will all kind of converge to roughly the same sort of level

insights.claim: The scenario that most worries Tchir is China loosening the leash on its AI entrepreneurs — Chinese engineers are currently hamstrung by having to follow the party line, and freedom to experiment would make them formidable.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A specific, observable trigger to monitor: Beijing shifting from directive to permissive AI policy would be the bear catalyst for US AI valuations.
insights.quote: no one wants to tell a dear leader that the party line's not working

insights.claim: AI has disappointed on its core promise — companies that spent heavily expecting headcount reduction still have to fact-check outputs and still need the employees, cooling initial enamorment.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Weak realized ROI plus high US token costs is the combination that makes enterprises defect to cheap Chinese models.
insights.quote: I spent X on AI and I still have to fact check and I still have to do all these I actually still need employee

insights.claim: US equity market valuation rests on the assumption that whatever AI capacity gets built will earn a return — an assumption cheap Chinese compute directly attacks.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: The single-sentence statement of the index-level risk: this is a market-cap concentration problem, not a sector problem.
insights.quote: our stock market valuation is so dependent right now on this assumption that whatever you build you will be earned something on

insights.claim: Semiconductor index price action is being distorted by market structure — triple-leveraged ETFs like SOXL plus single-name leveraged ETFs mechanically amplified the March-to-June rally driven by 'situational awareness' flows and the subsequent selloff, so the current bounce may not be real.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Treat semi rallies as flow-driven rather than fundamental; sell into strength after big bounces.
insights.quote: I'm not sure that I trust this bounce that we've seen whether it's real or whether it's still the unwind of situational awareness

insights.claim: Tchir's portfolio stance is a heavy underweight to semis/AI funded into equal-weight S&P 500, European equities, energy, and hyperscaler debt — with the twist that even if China wins on compute, it accelerates domestic chip and energy investment.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: The full trade expression of the episode: short concentration, long breadth and physical assets.
insights.quote: I want to underweight that sector heavily while I'm overweing some of the other things we've talked about.

themes.theme: Geographic winners: Americas, Canada, Europe, EM

insights.claim: Deglobalization's losers are the GCC states as the Gulf's share of global commerce shrinks, while net energy exporters — the US, Canada, Venezuela and Argentina — gain share.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A durable rotation in energy geography; Venezuela is early-stage because majors remain wary of interfering with existing lawsuits.

insights.claim: Canada gets a rare complete redo on LNG — it lost 15 years of opportunity to overregulation while the US captured the market, and is only now realizing the cost, per the CEO of TC Energy.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Canadian energy infrastructure is a deregulation-optionality trade with a European offtake buyer waiting.
insights.quote: Canada could have been really good at LG 15 years ago. The US could have been really good. The US got really good because they agreed to do it. Canada regulated.

insights.claim: European energy companies including Shell and Total should do very well because Europe must harness its own production and pivot to Canada and the US for energy sources.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Named European majors as a direct expression of the European energy-security capex cycle.

insights.claim: Investors should go global now — emerging markets should do very well, Poland (via EPOL) is a central hub if something finally breaks and gets fixed in Europe, and the equal-weight S&P 500 at all-time highs is preferable to cap-weighted.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Specific named vehicles for the anti-US-concentration trade; Poland is the leveraged play on European rearmament and reconstruction.
insights.quote: I still like Poland, EOL, EPOL as if something finally breaks and fixes in Europe. I think that's going to be a central hub.

insights.claim: Tariffing Canadian potash was an own goal that hurt US farmers with no offsetting benefit, and US relations with Canada and Mexico are likely to improve as a matter of necessity — possibly as part of a deal not to tariff things America cannot yet make itself.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: Positions Canadian and Mexican assets for a tariff-relief re-rating that consensus is not anticipating under this administration.
insights.quote: Tariffing pot ash has been an own goal, right? It's like we haven't really benefited much from it and we keep hurting our farmers.

insights.claim: Monroe Doctrine 2.0 is close to inevitable because a US reducing its global protection costs can still credibly defend the Western Hemisphere, making the Americas the natural integrated supply-chain bloc.
insights.speaker: Peter Tchir
insights.so_what: A hemispheric allocation framework: Latin American resources, logistics and manufacturing as the structural beneficiary of US retrenchment.
